problem: The blocks run control column → bell crank → both a rod and a cable loop → horn. This shows the rod and the cable as two branches hanging off the same bell crank, so a student may read it as one aircraft using both paths in series. A bell crank also belongs to the rod run, not to the start of a cable loop.
fix: Branch the two paths at the control column itself: column → (rod path: bell crank → push-pull rod) and column → (cable path: two-cable loop), with both meeting again at the surface horn. Label the branches 'alternative routes, not both fitted'.

problem: 'It removes side loads' is misleading. A spherical rod end cannot remove a side load; it simply carries axial load only, so any side load must be reacted by the guides or idler levers, and no bending moment is passed into the tube.
fix: Write: 'The ball lets the rod tilt a few degrees without bending the tube and carries axial load only, so no bending moment is passed into the tube; side loads are taken by the guides and idler levers.'

problem: 'Modern transports keep cables only as a backup or for secondary controls; the main path is fly-by-wire' overgeneralises. Many airliners in service today still use conventional cable and rod primary controls with hydraulic boost, and fly-by-wire is common mainly on newer designs.
fix: Write: 'On newer transports the main path is fly-by-wire, with cables kept as a backup or for secondary controls; many airliners in service still use boosted cable and rod primary controls.'
